name: okc-dashboard
description: Make a virtual machine, set it up, snapshot it, throw it away.
//main: An app page, loaded from disk. That is what makes NW.js behave normally: the page gets node, and the SDK build gives it a right-click Inspect of its own. Served over http instead it would be a remote page, which gets neither -- which is why nothing here has to hand-write a context menu.
//chromium-args: Deliberately none. The previous version passed --disable-features=nw2, which selects the older window implementation -- and under it NW.js's own nw.Window shim throws 'getRoutingID is not a function' on every page load, and native confirm() silently returns false. Nothing here needs the flag, so it is gone and both of those go with it. If something ever does need it, expect that error back.
//not--enable-node-worker: Node in Web Workers, usually paired with --mixed-context. There are no Web Workers here: the only one in the tree is Ace's syntax checker and it is turned off in both editors. The reason somebody would reach for it is that the window shares one node context, so a readFileSync or execFileSync in an action freezes the UI -- but a worker is not the fix for that. The actions table is one surface reached in-process on purpose, and putting it behind a worker means a message bridge, which is what core/ipc.js already is. If the freeze ever bites, make the file calls async, or let the window talk over the pipe.
//not--mixed-context: Merges the node and DOM contexts into one. It is the fix for cross-context type checks -- a node Buffer failing instanceof Uint8Array in the page, an Error from an action failing instanceof Error -- and this app has no instanceof anywhere in its own code and passes plain objects and JSON, reading e.message rather than testing types. So it would fix a problem written out of existence already. It is also not free: ui/ is ONE shared global scope by design, and merging node's globals into it widens the surface where a `const` here collides with something already declared. Checked: `find` is the only ui name that shadows a window property, and none shadow a node global -- so nothing is broken today, and the risk is what a new declaration costs tomorrow.
//logging: tools/nw.js passes --enable-logging=stderr, which is what makes the RENDERER audible -- the node context was always heard, the window never was. The bare --enable-logging writes the same lines to User Data/chrome_debug.log instead, and --v=1 adds three hundred lines of Chromium talking about itself. Measured; see the comment there.

scripts.test: node test/generic-test.js && node test/window-test.js && node test/declared-test.js && node test/events-test.js && node test/outline.js --check
scripts.//quit: Asks the running dashboard to close itself, rather than killing the process. The window loads server.js at startup, so a code change means a restart -- this is the half of that which was reaching for a process list.
scripts.//restart: Quit, wait until it is actually gone, and start again. The waiting is why this is a script and not `quit && start`: appQuit answers before it closes, so the old app still holds the port at the moment the reply arrives. See tools/restart.js.

//dependencies: None, and that is a property worth keeping rather than an accident. What this app uses beyond NW.js is checked in under vendors/ -- the Ace editor, xterm.js, marked and nanotar -- because a dependency resolved by a package manager is whatever the registry served the day somebody last installed it, and the same window on another machine is then not the same window. See vendors/README.md.
